name: Sampling Rate

claims.claim_text: Around 2011 the ultra-low-power 16-bit analog-to-digital converter segment held only about half a dozen usable parts, where ultra-low-power meant roughly 100 microwatts at an 8 kHz sample rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's like half a dozen choices in the ultra-low-power 16-bit analog-to-digital converter. And by ultra-low-power, I'm talking 100 microwatts
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: Low-power 16-bit converters are plentiful at very low speeds, with many topping out near 300 samples per second; pushing the same power budget to kilohertz sample rates sharply narrows the field of available parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can get lots of low-power 16-bit converters, but they all run at like 300 samples per second maximum or something like that.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: Converter power efficiency is usefully normalised as energy per sample rather than as bulk supply current; a part drawing about 100 microwatts at 8 kSa/s works out to roughly 0.1 picojoule per sample, or about 40 microamps from a 2.5 V rail.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's like 0.1 picajoules per sample or something
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Analog Devices, Design Spark - Unusual Usenet Usurpation

claims.claim_text: The Analog Devices AD7691 draws about 108 microwatts at an 8 kHz sample rate and delivers 18 bits rather than the 16 bits its class implies, making it a benchmark low-power converter for kilohertz-rate acquisition.
claims.quote_verbatim: And it takes 108 microwatts at 8 kilohertz sample rate.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chairs, Sparks and Devices - Optional Olent Obreption

claims.claim_text: A precision analog-to-digital converter is defined by its accuracy at DC, not by its speed; headline gigasample-per-second parts sit at the opposite end of the design space and may not measure a static volt accurately.
claims.quote_verbatim: that is actually the definition of a precision analog to digital converter, is that it's accurate at DC
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Silego, ADCs & Seismic Detection - Dave's Dingo Dystocia

claims.claim_text: Top-end oscilloscopes running at 40 gigasamples per second per channel depend on sampling clocks that are both very high frequency and very low jitter, pushing the oscillator design into exotic materials and physics.
claims.quote_verbatim: 40 gig sample per second. 40 gig, yeah. Each channel. Yeah, you figure you have to have a very high rate of, you know, oscillator. And it's got to be really precise too.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: Oscilloscope high-resolution mode averages groups of adjacent samples on the fly, typically four or ten, trading effective sample rate for lower noise; it is appropriate only when the signal under test does not need the instrument's full sample rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can use the high res mode these days, which implements the on-the-fly averaging, you know, between like four samples or ten samples or something
claims.speaker: Alan Wolke

claims.claim_text: Aliasing is the condition in which distinct input frequencies become indistinguishable after conversion, determined by the relationship between the frequency of interest and the sampling rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: aliasing is when different frequencies appear to be the same once they're converted
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: Understanding data converters requires moving fluently between the time domain and the frequency domain, because some converter behaviours are only visible in one representation.
claims.quote_verbatim: To really, really understand converters, you have to be able to go back and forth between the two pretty easily.
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: In the frequency domain, sliding the analog input frequency upward relative to a fixed sampling rate makes the alias images move downward, in the opposite direction.
claims.quote_verbatim: how when you slide the analog frequency up relative to the sampling rate, how the aliases then move in the opposite direction
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: Aliasing can be demonstrated in the time domain by sampling three sine waves of different frequencies at one common rate: one cycle in ten samples, eleven cycles in the same ten slots, and twenty-one cycles in the same ten slots all produce identical sample values.
claims.quote_verbatim: The lower frequency, 10 samples converts to one cycle of the input. In the middle one, 11 cycles will fit in those same 10 slots. And in the top one, 21 cycles fit in the same slot.
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: Sampled time-domain data should be plotted as discrete points rather than as connected line segments, because connecting the dots invites the viewer to infer waveform detail that the sample set does not actually contain.
claims.quote_verbatim: trying to get people to plot their time domain digital signals as distinct points instead of connecting the dots with lines
claims.speaker: Hank Zumbahlen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Hank Zumbahlen - Zoppa Zumbahlen Zateticism

claims.claim_text: A low-cost analog-plus-digital capture device specified at 12 megasamples per second across eight channels at 10 bits yields roughly 600 kHz of usable analog bandwidth; the bandwidth figure, not the sample rate, is the specification that determines what such an instrument can actually resolve.
claims.quote_verbatim: It has a 12 mic sample per second converter, eight channels at 10 bits. Yeah. So, 600 kilohertz bandwidth. That's what I really care.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: We're Sorry! But Apple Ain't! - Remorseless RAM Racketeering

claims.claim_text: A front end that streams 20 megasamples per second continuously over USB makes a poor oscilloscope but a serviceable data-acquisition instrument, because the value of continuous streaming is uninterrupted record length rather than peak timing resolution.
claims.quote_verbatim: it wouldn't be a terrific oscilloscope because it's only 20 mega samples per second, but it streams those samples to, you know, over USB continuously
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: The alternative architecture to continuous streaming is to sample far faster than the host link can carry, apply triggering and local storage, and then read the captured record out slowly over the interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do something with a much higher sample rate and do triggering and storage and stuff and then, you know, slowly stream the samples over USB
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: In a memoryless streaming radio front end the achievable sample rate is set by the host interface rather than by the converters, so the maximum throughput of high-speed USB becomes the governing design constraint for the whole signal chain.
claims.quote_verbatim: my primary limitation and the limitation that hacker one is designed around is the, the maximum speed of high speed USB
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Pairs of 8-bit quadrature samples delivered 20 million times per second essentially saturate high-speed USB, which fixes the instantaneous bandwidth of such a receiver at about 20 MHz.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm getting a pair of eight bit samples, 20 million times per second. And that pretty much maxes out high speed USB.
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: A 20 megasample-per-second design point sits at a favourable cost break, because analog and digital signal-chain components rated meaningfully faster than that become substantially more expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: finding components that would really do the job much faster than that, end up being a lot more expensive
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: In chirp radar the sample rate purchases unambiguous range extent: a coffee-can radar limited to a roughly 15 kHz audio input reaches only about 100 to 150 metres, whereas raising the sample rate extends detection of car-sized 10 dBsm targets out to about a kilometre.
claims.quote_verbatim: sample rates buy you on chirp radar systems is, is you get a larger range extent
claims.speaker: Gregory Charvat
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Effective number of bits falls as sample rate rises within a single converter: one measurement chain delivers about 18 effective bits at 8 kSa/s but recovers to over 19 bits at around 100 samples per second.
claims.quote_verbatim: so at, at 8 K, then it's down at 18 and at, uh, like a hundred or so, then it's, it's back up to 19 point something
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Streaming analog capture at 50 megasamples per second consumes host RAM so quickly that even a machine with 8 to 16 GB is limited to roughly 20 to 30 seconds of continuous recording, whereas compressed digital channels can be recorded for days.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're recording analog at a high sample rate, like you're going to be limited to like maybe 20 or 30 seconds of recording
claims.speaker: Mark Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: The highest real-time bandwidth oscilloscope available in the mid-2010s was a 100 GHz instrument sampling at 240 gigasamples per second with 8-bit resolution, a product of the Teledyne LeCroy line.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a 100 gigahertz bandwidth real-time scope that samples 240 giga samples a second at 8-bit resolution.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Bogatin - Tilded Thumb Tenets

claims.claim_text: Audio converter product definition often reduces to whether basic functions such as switching between 44.1 kHz and 48 kHz sample rates are exposed on hardware pins or over a serial bus; many hardware customers insist on a pin they can pull low even when I2C or SPI control would unlock more features.
claims.quote_verbatim: all you want to do is switch from, like, 44.1 to 48K
claims.speaker: Dafydd Roche

claims.claim_text: A video DAC clocked at 30 MHz yields a usable output analog bandwidth on the order of 5 MHz, since reconstruction filtering and sin(x)/x roll-off consume most of the nominal Nyquist span.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think if 30 MHz is a sample rate, then the output analog bandwidth might be, like, 5 MHz or something, right?

claims.claim_text: A recommended development sequence for a high-speed output stage is to prove the system with an 8-bit DAC first, confirming how fast the whole chain runs, and only then move to a 12-bit or 16-bit part.
claims.quote_verbatim: Well, I would start with the 8-bit DAC, because then it's, you know, a matter of you can see how fast it all works.

claims.claim_text: A handheld oscilloscope specified at 100 MHz analog bandwidth with 500 megasamples per second illustrates the conventional five-to-one relationship between sample rate and rated bandwidth in mid-range instruments.
claims.quote_verbatim: 100 meg analog bandwidth, 500 meg samples per second.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Reference designs supply only the minimum support circuitry needed for one assumed operating point, so an ADC front end copied unchanged will carry the wrong anti-aliasing filter as soon as the sample rate is altered.
claims.quote_verbatim: But if you're using a different sample rate, bingo, your anti-aliasing filter is going to be different, for example.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: General-purpose microcontrollers increasingly carry digital audio interfaces; the ESP32 provides two channels of I2S output capable of 24-bit data at sample rates beyond hi-fi requirements, enough for one device to drive several audio channels.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has two channels, uh, of I2S output that is able to deliver, uh, um, uh, 24 bits
claims.speaker: Jørgen Jakobsen

claims.claim_text: Oscilloscope bandwidth and sample rate are frequently gated in firmware rather than hardware, and unlocking them can push a unit's sample rate above the maximum specified for any model in its product family, though the resulting acquisition is not necessarily calibrated.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was able to up the sample rate above what the maximum they specify in any of their 1000X products
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: An instrument rated 100 megasamples per second but only 30 MHz of bandwidth runs at roughly three times oversampling where a factor of ten is the usual rule of thumb; such a ratio still avoids reporting an incorrect frequency but gives poor waveform fidelity.
claims.quote_verbatim: it says it's 100 mega samples, but then I think they list the bandwidth at 30 megahertz, but then, that's pretty rough. I mean, like, that's only a third of the sample rate, right? Yeah, yeah. So usually you do a tenth.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: When sin(x)/x interpolation is applied to the captured record, a sample rate of only about 2.4 times the bandwidth is mathematically sufficient to reconstruct the input waveform exactly.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're doing sine x on x interpolation, you only need 2.4 times.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Look at nature and meet nerds

claims.claim_text: Dedicating one acquisition ASIC per oscilloscope channel preserves 6.25 gigasamples per second on every channel simultaneously; by contrast many instruments halve or quarter the sample rate as additional channels are switched on, and per-channel converters cannot be ganged to double the rate on one channel.
claims.quote_verbatim: a good lot of scopes out there will halve the sample rate, for example, if you turn on a second channel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Resolution and sample rate trade against each other inside a single acquisition system: a 12-bit oscilloscope front end may sustain full resolution only up to about 3 gigasamples per second while reaching higher rates at reduced bit depth.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a 12-bit converter, but I think it only goes to 3 gig at 12 bits.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The LeCroy HDO8000A series, released in 2017, offered eight 12-bit channels at 10 gigasamples per second plus an external trigger and a separate 16-channel logic analyzer, and drove an external ultra-HD monitor so that all channels could be displayed at once.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's higher sample rate, 10 gig instead of 6.5 gig.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Successive-approximation converters built for precision applications typically top out around five megasamples per second, with faster conversion handled by separate high-speed product families.
claims.quote_verbatim: the SAR converters that, you know, that at least are from my precision group are, um, usually about five mega samples, um, is the, the max.
claims.speaker: Art Kay

claims.claim_text: Converter precision degrades as conversion rate increases, which is why precision and high-speed converters are developed as distinct product lines rather than as points on one continuum.
claims.quote_verbatim: I guess, I guess the precision starts to fall off as you go faster and faster too.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Conventional smart-meter chips built around fixed-function DSP blocks are limited to roughly three to six kilohertz of measurement bandwidth, whereas a software-defined metering front end can sample up to a megasample per second and resolve far more harmonic content.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're somewhere between, uh, a three and six kilohertz bandwidth

claims.claim_text: In GNU Radio the core signal-processing blocks are written in C++ with only a Python interface layer on top, because high-end and commercial systems run at sample rates that demand direct access to the machine architecture for optimisation.
claims.quote_verbatim: we are talking about potentially massive sample rates here in some of the more commercial or high-end research systems and the c++ gives you that

claims.claim_text: The Keysight UXR series reaches a true 110 GHz of real-time bandwidth on all channels at roughly 256 gigasamples per second, using an indium phosphide front end rather than silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: It is true 110 gig bandwidth. With I think 250 gig sample per second.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A current-measurement instrument sampling at only 4 kilosamples per second, with a range from one microamp to five amps, cannot capture the fast current slugs that dominate battery-powered radio designs, where a device sleeps most of the time and a LoRa transmit burst alone draws 20 milliamps or more.
claims.quote_verbatim: the Koitek one is only 4k samples per second and it's only one, one microamps to five amps.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A logic analyzer in timing analysis mode behaves like an oscilloscope with a comparator front end, sampling asynchronously at a fixed rate such as 50 or 100 megasamples per second and rendering the result as blocky square transitions.
claims.quote_verbatim: It works like an oscilloscope. It just samples. At a fixed sample rate.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Sampling a 50 MHz design with a 200 megasample-per-second logic analyzer gives only four times oversampling, which is enough to capture the states but not enough time granularity to resolve the setup and hold relationships between signals, so a much higher oversample rate is needed for timing debug.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you've got four times there. So you've got enough. Right. But then. You don't have enough granulation. To start then seeing the timing differences.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because a logic analyzer's sampling clock and the design under test are not synchronised, the two drift relative to each other over minutes; a circuit can appear to work and then suddenly show nonsense as edges drift out of the sampling window, an artefact easily mistaken for a real intermittent fault.
claims.quote_verbatim: Those two clocks aren't precisely synchronized. Right. So they're going to slowly drift with respect to each other.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: When a digital capture shows an anomaly, the first question is whether it is genuine circuit behaviour, noise, or an artefact of undersampling; correctly configured logic thresholds do not eliminate the risk, because real switching levels shift with temperature and part grade and a runt pulse that barely reaches the threshold can cost weeks of troubleshooting.
claims.quote_verbatim: Are you looking at noise? Are you looking at. Some kind of. Actual aberration. Or is it just that. Your samples are way out.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Boxcar averaging is a rolling-average filter applied to samples immediately after the ADC stage, before display processing, which raises the effective number of bits; an oscilloscope with only an 8-bit converter can present 9, 10, 11 or 12 bits of resolution this way.
claims.quote_verbatim: by averaging your samples, you can get a higher effective number of bits

claims.claim_text: Gaining effective resolution through averaging costs sample rate: the instrument's effective sample rate drops in proportion to the number of samples combined per displayed point.
claims.quote_verbatim: Do you lower your sample rate because, like, your effective sample rate drops then too? You do effectively lower your, yeah.

claims.claim_text: In an I2S audio system the master clock must be an integer multiple of the sampling frequency and a much higher one; a 50 MHz sampling bandwidth oversampled 64 times would demand a 3.2 GHz clock, comparable to a high-end processor core clock and prohibitive on power grounds.
claims.quote_verbatim: So your clock frequency has to be an integer multiple of your sampling frequency.
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: A sigma-delta converter samples in a very small window and continuously compares the input against its running estimate, using a one-bit DAC fed back through an integrator and summing junction; the resulting average is highly accurate, which is why sigma-delta sampling frequencies sit orders of magnitude above the signal band.
claims.quote_verbatim: the principle of, of a Sigma Delta DAC or Sigma Delta ADC is that you take some small sampling window and you basically determine if you are over that point or under it constantly
claims.speaker: Nash Reilly

claims.claim_text: Triggering exists because capturing every event at the rate needed to resolve millisecond-scale phenomena over days produces unmanageable data volumes; the trigger provides the rule for discarding irrelevant samples once the acquisition buffer fills.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's the reason triggering exists because you have to have some other way to throw away
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Oscilloscopes and logic analyzers default to 50 percent pre-trigger and 50 percent post-trigger capture so that the record shows the conditions leading up to the trigger event as well as its aftermath.
claims.quote_verbatim: every scope by default has 50% pre and post triggering and every logic analyzer 50% because you want to see what happened before that trigger event
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: MATLAB's FVTool plots a digital filter's response from DC to Nyquist and requires the sampling rate to be entered, since the frequency axis of any discrete-time filter is meaningful only relative to that rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: it just shows it from, you know, DC to, to Nyquist, uh, is all, is all it does. Cause it, cause you, you, you, you have to punch in what your, uh, what your sampling rate and all that is.

claims.claim_text: A current-measurement instrument sampling two million times per second resolves firmware changes of a few milliseconds in a power waveform, letting a developer quantify the energy saved by shortening a routine.
claims.quote_verbatim: sampling at two million times a second, it makes it really easy to see
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: At audio sample rates of 44.1 or 48 kHz, one sample period leaves room for on the order of a thousand processing operations on a fast DSP, so feed-forward loudspeaker correction is straightforward; closing a loop from the loudspeaker output back to the amplifier input demands latency low enough to require custom silicon instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: even on, on a fast enough DSP between two samples of audio, you can do a thousand, uh, processing operations
claims.episode_title: High End Audio with Remco Stoutjesdijk

claims.claim_text: A digital multimeter samples at a fixed interval and shows only the converted value, so rapidly changing circuit values fall between samples and are never displayed; bar-graph secondary displays exist to restore that dynamic feel, with a 105-step graph giving one percent resolution at about ten updates per second.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because DMM samples at a fixed time interval. Changing values in a circuit are often lost.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The Nyquist criterion sets a floor of two times the highest frequency of interest, while the common instrument rule of thumb is roughly ten times the bandwidth in order to see waveform detail rather than merely avoid aliasing.
claims.quote_verbatim: you better go above Nyquist if you ever want to see something. 10x, Nyquist is usually pretty good
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: For an oscilloscope with a Gaussian frequency response, a sample rate of about 2.3 times the rated bandwidth is sufficient to guarantee no aliasing, so a 100 MHz instrument needs roughly 230 megasamples per second.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can get away with only 2.3 times above the bandwidth as sample rate. So if you're sampling, so if your bandwidth's 100 megahertz, you need 230, 230 meg samples per second.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Some high-speed oscilloscopes from major vendors ship with sample rates below twice their rated bandwidth, so the sample-rate-to-bandwidth ratio should be checked directly rather than assumed from the headline bandwidth figure.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know for a fact that high speed scopes from some of the big guys are not even two times.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Audio marketing pushes 24-bit converters running at nearly 200 kHz sample rates when far lower specifications are adequate; the engineering task is to trace the requirement back to what is actually audible, since the difference between a $30 and a $2 DAC is often inaudible in the finished product.
claims.quote_verbatim: 24 bit analog digital converters running at almost 200 kilohertz of a sample rate when it actually comes down to it, you know, much low is even fine
claims.speaker: Philip Salmony
claims.episode_title: Mixed Signal Education with Philip Salmony

claims.claim_text: Very cheap pocket oscilloscopes expose beginners to aliasing artefacts before they have the experience to recognise them, so a sub-par instrument makes early debugging harder rather than easier.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to run into things like anti-alising and just other stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Between the roughly $400 and $800 tiers of four-channel oscilloscopes the incremental purchase is a larger touchscreen, higher sample rates and more acquisition memory; for general bench use a $400 four-channel instrument remains adequate indefinitely.
claims.quote_verbatim: You get higher sample rates. You get more memory.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An open-source oscilloscope front end built around the HMCAD1511 four-channel ADC achieves about one gigasample per second with roughly 350 MHz of analog bandwidth, with proper shielding cans in the front end.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got a HAD 1511 ADC, four channel ADC. I think it's only one gig sample per second. But I think it's 350 meg analog bandwidth.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A bulk capacitor sitting where a battery connects to a board forms a low-pass filter in the current path, so the current waveform reaching the measurement instrument is already smoothed regardless of how fast the instrument samples.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've automatically created a really nice low pass filter
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: One current-measurement instrument samples internally at 250 kilosamples per second but presents at most 50 kilosamples per second to the user, averaging five by five, because the extra rate is not needed for most measurements.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're sampling at 250 kilo samples a second we're actually only presenting 50 kilo samples a second at the moment as the maximum number of samples that you can see so they're all averaged out 5x5
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Sleep-current measurement needs only hundreds of samples per second, or even one per second; the practical architecture keeps a slow default rate and switches to a high-speed mode only when an event of interest occurs.
claims.quote_verbatim: measuring sleep currents you want even less I mean you want hundreds of samples a second or even one per second
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: Measurement requirements should be right-sized against their cost, since instruments capable of picoamp resolution are priced for semiconductor work rather than board-level electronics design.
claims.quote_verbatim: square your monetary expectations towards your measurement needs and right size yourself
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: The Tektronix TBS1000 series pairs a one gigasample-per-second acquisition rate with only about 20 kilopoints of sample memory, a combination that illustrates how a high headline sample rate says nothing about usable record length.
claims.quote_verbatim: 20K of sample memory. So that might be a variation on the, on, on that ASIC
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: When a synthesised tone frequency falls at an exact order of the sampling frequency, the same phase point is sampled every period and the output collapses to a constant, transmitting nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd sample a zero at the same time you're trying to sample your signal every single time. So you just get all zeros.
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Choosing the sampling frequency for a one-bit synthesised carrier is an art of maximising the number of transitions in the output pattern, because the transmitted energy comes from the switching between on and off rather than from the sample values themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is a little bit of an art of, of selecting a sampling frequency such that like you get the most number of ones and zeros
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: A low-cost FPGA such as the Tang Nano 9K is only marginally fast enough to accept 50 to 100 megasamples per second from an external ADC and simultaneously drive a parallel TFT display, making sample-rate throughput the binding constraint in a hobby oscilloscope build.
claims.quote_verbatim: the capabilities of the 9k are barely fast enough like to get input from that adc in 50 or 100 mega samples and then display it on the tft
claims.speaker: Bitluni

claims.claim_text: USB oscilloscopes have long offered 12-bit and even 16-bit converters, because bit depth is cheap at modest speeds; the scarce quantity is bandwidth, meaning resolution sustained at a high sample rate.
claims.quote_verbatim: 12-bits were always a thing in USB scopes, right? USB scopes – 12-bits, like even 16-bits are still a thing. But it's bandwidth, right?
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: High converter resolution is straightforward to obtain if the sample rate is allowed to drop; a 24-bit ADC can be placed in an oscilloscope provided the acquisition is slowed down, so the engineering difficulty lies in holding resolution at speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: anyone can do 16 – but you put a 24-bit ADC in the scope if you want. Slow it down.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
